newsitem.title: USA: A new "Titanic" - will songs make it float this time?.
newsitem.headline: A new "Titanic" - will songs make it float this time?.

text.p: Given the precarious and costly nature of mounting a Broadway musical these days, it might be tempting fate -- not to mention critics -- to announce a new show called "Titanic."
Yet a host of veterans from Broadway and London's West End are already on board the project slated for the spring of 1997, producers announced recently.

Peter Stone, who was scored in the past with "1776", "Woman of the Year" and "The Will Rogers Follies" -- Tony winners all -- will write the book while music and lyrics will come from Maury Yeston of "Nine" and "Grand Hotel" fame.

The heart of the show will revolve around six main characters -- a stoker, a lookout and a radioman, as well as the captain, the builder and the owner of the Titanic, a British liner that sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg in the North Atlantic killing more than 1,500 people. No casting details were available as yet.

But from the initial material made available, it sounds as though the show will replicate the opulent, lavish style of the world's largest ship that boasted such passengers as John Jacob Astor on its fateful, maiden voyage from Southhampton, England, to New York.

It will contrast the free-living lifestyle of the wealthy passengers who danced the evening away in sartorial splendor amid endless cocktails, while below even the immigrants in steerage enjoyed an unprecedented four days of leisure.
Until April 14, 1912, that is, and that iceberg. A perfect denouement for Act I, it would seem -- crunch!

Act II? As the disaster becomes real, there seems great opportunity for sort of lavish, effect-ridden trappings that have made long-lasting hits of "Phamtom of the Opera," "Miss Saigon" and "Les Miserables." San Francisco, after all, just completed a run of "The Towering Inferno" -- on stage.

Nevertheless a bit of substance will apparently be injected into "Titanic," "as 19th-Century civilisation, with its corseted morality, its extravagant codes of honour and sacrifice, its unswerving belief that God favoured the rich, plunged that night to the bottom of the sea," according to early material.

British theatre and opera director Richard Jones is set to helm the voyage to Broadway sometime in March 1997, with an opening the following month at the Lunt-Fontanne theatre, recently home to Carol Channing's revival tour of "Hello, Dolly!"
No word yet on any special promotions. Women and children half-price, perhaps? Or maybe walk-on roles for survivors.

Titanic-mania peaked again recently with the attemp to raise a portion of the bow which ended in failure when a cable snapped and the wreckage plunged back to its watery grave, disappointing thousands of buffs who had taken cruises to the site to view the historic event.

The wreckage was first discovered in 1985 about 300 miles (480 km) southeast of Newfoundland, Canada. Since then the notion of salvaging wreckage and other items such as china from the Titanic has been controversial, with some maintaining it is akin to grave robbing.
Others maintain it is history which should be studied as closely as possible.
